Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA View image in fullscreen The shuttered Saudi embassy in Yemen’s capital Sana’a, with a mural depicting a Houthi fighter stopping a ship. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA Yemen Houthis claim attack on Saudi base as fighting flares with Yemeni forces Iran-allied Houthis say drones and missiles used in attack that targeted ‘weapons depots and command and control centres’ in southern Saudi Arabia Agence France-Presse Sat 12 Sep 2026 21.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Houthi fighters on Sunday said they used drones and missiles to attack a military base in southern Saudi Arabia as renewed fighting with Yemen’s government forces led growing numbers of civilians to flee . The attack at the southern Sharurah base targeted “weapons depots and command and control centres that are managing the aggression against our nation and people”, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree wrote on X. The date of the operation was not specified. Clashes have increased this week between the Iran-allied Houthis and Yemeni government forces, which are backed by Riyadh. On Saturday, the government forces said they had struck Houthi fighters in the Red Sea city of Mocha, and later attacked other Houthi positions in the south-western part of the country. “Air Force of the Armed Forces targeted positions and barracks of the terrorist Houthi group with three airstrikes” in the Taiz region, the Yemeni military said Sunday in a post on X. The rapid Houthi advance in Yemen: why it matters and what’s at stake Read more The US news site Axios also reported that Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman twice called Donald Trump to request strikes on the Houthis last week, but that the request was rejected. The ongoing clashes follow a week-long Houthi offensive that culminated in the group capturing the remainder of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and several strategic islands, cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab strait at the sea’s southern entrance. The waterway has become an important artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports after Iran largely cut off shipments through the Gulf with its blockade on the strait of Hormuz at the start of the Middle East war. The Houthis have recently declared their own maritime blockade of Riyadh’s Red Sea ports. The government news agency Saba reported on Saturday that Yemeni “forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia” near the port of Mocha, and quoted a spokesperson for the forces as saying they had also struck Houthi targets just outside the city. The Houthis, meanwhile, said on Saturday evening that over the past 48 hours, “Saudi enemy aircraft conducted 129 airstrikes” on areas under their control. Yemen’s civil war, which began in 2014 with the Houthi capture of the capital Sana’a, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022 but roared back to life in July. Saudi Arabia first entered the war on the side of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in 2015 and continues to support the Aden-based administration. On Saturday night, Saudi authorities said a Houthi projectile fell in an area near the border, hours after issuing alerts warning of the risk of possible attacks. The civil defence directorate said the incident resulted “in two injuries and material damage to a mosque, several buildings, and vehicles”. The Yemeni civil war has uprooted millions of people, and the latest fighting has led even more to flee their homes. The fall of Mocha to the Houthis on Thursday drove many residents to Aden, where the internationally recognised Yemeni government is based. The UN’s migration agency said on Saturday that 76,000 people had fled the fighting since July, a figure that had quadrupled since last week. About 1,400 people had fled to Djibouti, the country’s minister of economy and finance Ilyas Moussa Dawaleh said on Saturday. The renewed fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides. Trump on Saturday acknowledged speaking to the de facto Saudi leader but said the Houthis had also “called us and they don’t want to fight with us”. He did not elaborate on whether Washington would take any action, but told reporters that “everything’s gonna work out fine and dandy” in the region. In 2025, the US conducted a seven-week bombing campaign against the Houthis in response to their repeated attacks on Red Sea shipping in support of Hamas in the Gaza war. That ended with a negotiated ceasefire, though the Houthis kept up their missile and drone attacks targeting Israel. More recently, the group has resumed attacks on ships in the Red Sea after declaring their maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia. In Yemen’s capital Sana’a, Houthi supporters celebrated the freeing of 210 prisoners held in areas that fell to the group and had spent up to eight years in jail. In September, the infamous ShinyHunters hacking group claimed it had infiltrated the FBI job recruitment portal, stealing confidential data from 5,000 employees and even replacing the FBI logo with its own. The group has been implicated in hacking numerous large, high-profile organizations over the years, from the European Commission to Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar Games and the software firm behind Canvas.

Now, Reuters reports that a suspected leader of the group, a teenager named Saif al-Din Khader, is being detained in Jordan. Al-Din Khader—who uses the name Rey online—is said to be cooperating with the authorities, helping the FBI and global law enforcement to find the other hackers in the group, according to sources who spoke to Reuters.

According to independent security researcher Brian Krebs, Rey is responsible for releasing a ransomware strain known as ShinySp1d3r and was the administrator of the data leak website for Hellcat, a ransomware group linked to attacks on Schneider Electric, Telefonica, and Orange Romania.

You May Also Like

The FBI has yet to officially confirm the reports. Last month, FBI Director Kash Patel claimed another member of the group had been detained in the Netherlands, who Krebs says is named Pepijn van der Stap. Meanwhile, earlier this week, Reuters reported that ShinyHunters' dark web site had disappeared. Patel said on X earlier this week that the FBI's teams are working on new leads and that more arrests "are on the table."

ShinyHunters says it doesn't plan to ransom the stolen data and that it is not an act of extortion, claiming the attack "was all a marketing campaign to protect our business and actively combat disinformation." The group instead demanded that the FBI remove a public advisory it issued about the group in May 2026, which said the hackers often exaggerated their claims of access to victims' data.

Photograph: Stefano Porta/LaPresse/AP View image in fullscreen A fire burns following clashes between police and protesters in front of Milan’s cathedral on Saturday. Photograph: Stefano Porta/LaPresse/AP Italy Milan braces for more unrest as debate intensifies over Italy’s ‘lost generation’ Protests and fringe violence expose sharp divide between marginalised and immigrant youth and those with greater prospects Angela Giuffrida in Milan Fri 23 Oct 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google M artina Miccichè was filming riot police kicking and beating a teenager with batons as they dragged him along Piazza del Duomo, the central Milan square hosting its cathedral, when she was struck by a flying object, causing a deep gash and bruising near her right eye. The journalist had joined hundreds of mostly young people marching through the northern Italian city on Saturday afternoon to protest over soaring living costs and unaffordable housing, echoing the wider wave of economic discontent fuelling protests across Europe . It wasn’t the first time Italy’s youth have loudly aired their grievances during Giorgia Meloni’s four years as prime minister, despite the risk of falling foul of her ruling coalition’s ever-expanding crackdown on security and public dissent. On Saturday afternoon they plan to protest again in Milan and other major Italian cities. View image in fullscreen Youth protesters clash with police in Piazza del Duomo on Sunday, the second day of unrest in Milan. Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Miccichè said the atmosphere last Saturday was peaceful until about 5pm, when police blocked access to Via Broletto, a street about a 10-minute walk away from Piazza del Duomo. “People were angry because they were being repressed,” she said, claiming the police turned “suddenly violent” as they pushed the crowd back with their shields. “The violence escalated. They started to grab people at random, hitting and kicking them. It was shocking.” As the clashes continued and police filled the square with teargas while astonished tourists looked on, a group of masked youths on the fringes headed to the surrounding fashion district, tearing down road signs, setting bins alight and smashing shop windows – among them Footlocker and Levi’s – then looting them. View image in fullscreen Fires were lit in Piazza del Duomo on Saturday during the looting and vandalism. Photograph: Stefano Porta/LaPresse/Shutterstock The vandalism resumed on Sunday as the gangs – many baited by the promise of luxury goods through a network of social media chats – descended on the city centre again, mostly from marginalised areas on the outskirts. During the two days of unrest, police detained more than 271 young people. Of those, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals. As the Italian media published images of injured police officers, Meloni’s government rapidly enacted more measures targeting minors and further empowering the police – including holding parents financially accountable for their children’s vandalism and looting – while dispatching 500 troops to Milan. View image in fullscreen Clashes with police continued on Sunday in a second day of unrest in Milan. Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock The latest legislation also criminalises violent participation in ⁠a demonstration and toughens penalties for ⁠rioters. Some of the government’s security measures are now being applied in the south of Italy , where lorry drivers have been protesting against high petrol prices for more than a week, blocking roads and disrupting supermarket supplies. In response, 71 people have been reported to judicial authorities and 242 fined over the blockades – a protest act made illegal in a previous security bill. A government official also warned the lorry drivers that obstructing public highways could carry jail terms. View image in fullscreen Truck drivers blocked streets and tram tracks near the port of Naples on Thursday during a protest against increased fuel costs that began on 16 October. Photograph: Eliano Imperato/AFP/Getty Images “This government just tries to repress protesters instead of listening to them and addressing the issues,” said Miccichè, who needed stitches for her injury. “It is all connected. There is anger in the south over fuel prices and young people everywhere are angry – they don’t even have a chance to think about the future because they are so terrified of the present.” Furthermore, “we are not feeling safe”, the 34-year-old added, “because we can see how much space the police have now and how shielded they are”. Racial profiling had become the norm in Milan, especially in the centre and close to its train stations, she claimed. View image in fullscreen Young demonstrators faced teargas and water cannon in Turin on Saturday. Photograph: Daniele Solavaggione/LaPresse/Shutterstock The weekend’s urban unrest, including protests in Turin and Bologna, has intensified debate over Italy’s “lost generation”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Furthermore, the youth protests and subsequent fringe violence have exposed the sharp divide between Italy’s marginalised and immigrant youth and those with greater prospects. Working-class Italians or third- and second-generation immigrants are regularly labelled by rightwing politicians and the press as maranza , a derogatory term used to describe groups of young people who usually congregate in city centres. They come from areas like Barona, a sprawling council estate in the south-west of Milan. Young people there have been reflecting on the events of last weekend. “There is a lot of discontent – we are all children of this widespread malaise,” said Domenico Ricci, who along with Luca Orlando manages a bar that is part of Barrio’s , a cultural hub where the district’s youth come together. View image in fullscreen Protesters clash with police in Piazza del Duomo, Milan, on Sunday. Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Orlando believes the vandalism and looting were a symptom of anger and years of feeling unheard and invisible. “So when an opportunity arises, these kids take revenge. They don’t do it simply because they want to steal something. All this government does is introduce new crimes – they never listen or engage in dialogue.” Orlando, whose parents came from Calabria, is feeling the nationwide discontent. “But the protests there [in the south-west] have hardly had any coverage,” he said. “And we are only talking about Milan because of the violence and not the real issues.” Thomas, 18, who has grown up in Barona, is training to be a chef and wants to leave Italy “as soon as possible”. He said: “I see no future here.” His friend Mohamed, an Italian citizen of Moroccan origin, is still at high school and wants to become a lawyer. “If you make a mistake, then you must pay,” he said. “But this is also a characteristic of protests – the more a government doesn’t listen, the more people get angry.” Mauro Magatti, a sociologist at Milan’s Catholic University of the Sacred Heart, said socioeconomic discomfort and a sense of abandonment affected “an entire generation” and responding to the anger with excessive repression risked enlarging the protest. “Violence always needs to be condemned but now we need to lower the tone to overcome this burst of anger and violence and focus on addressing the real problems,” he said. View image in fullscreen Rightwing demonstrators held a ‘zero tolerance’ protest in Milan on Wednesday as law enforcement stepped up its presence. Photograph: Andrea Carrubba/Anadolu/Getty Images Police and military presence in central Milan has been building in recent days before Saturday’s protest, organised by a new online movement which has pledged to gather each weekend “until this government of thieves falls”. Security guards stood outside shops that had been damaged or looted last weekend. Italy’s politicians from across the spectrum must take heed, warned Miccichè, as the protests were only set to amplify ahead of general elections next year. “There is no perception at all of how young people feel,” she said. “Even if they took just a minute to listen, they will understand that it is a generation full of ideas – they just want to be heard.” Explore more on these topics Italy Protest Cost of living crisis Activism Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Macron bans ‘illegitimate’ protests in France as he tries to get a grip on unrest Angry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting cases Europe’s far right seizes on protest violence to push authoritarian anti-immigration agenda Macron accuses Trump and other foreign leaders of ‘stupid comments’ about France unrest Why are French police so violent?
